chapter.title: Your three accounts

cards.body: If your broker's app shut down tomorrow, your shares would not vanish with it. They were never there. In the bazaar you need three things: a purse for cash (your bank account), a runner who carries your order to the stalls (your trading account, run by a *broker*), and a locker that holds what you bought (your *demat account*). **The runner never keeps your shares. The locker does.**

cards.prompt: Priya buys 1 share of Infosys through a broker app in March. In June the broker shuts down for good. Where is her share?

options.text: Gone. It lived inside the app.
Sitting in her demat locker at NSDL or CDSL, untouched.
Turned back into cash in her bank account.

whyNot.a: That's the runner, not the locker: the app only carried the order. The share went into a locker the broker does not own.
whyNot.c: That's the purse, not the locker: cash lives in the bank, shares live in the demat account. Nothing turns into cash unless she sells.

cards.reteach: Three places, three jobs. The bank holds rupees. The broker's trading account is a counter where you place orders. The share itself is stored in a demat account at one of India's two national lockers, NSDL or CDSL, in Priya's name. The broker can close; the locker stays.

cards.title: Three accounts, three jobs
cards.body:
Your *bank account* is the purse. Rupees sit there until you decide to buy.

Your *trading account* is the counter at a broker's stall. You type an order there, and the broker, a SEBI-registered middleman, walks it into the exchange for you. Cash moves from the bank to this counter just before you buy, and back after you sell.

Your *demat account* is the locker. Demat is short for *dematerialised*: your shares are electronic entries, not paper certificates. The locker is run by NSDL or CDSL, India's two depositories, and it is in your name. **The broker opens the locker for you. It does not own what's inside.**

cards.title: Ravi's Sunday evening
cards.body:
Ravi opens his accounts on a Sunday night from his sofa: PAN card, Aadhaar, a blurry selfie, a signature drawn with his thumb, and his bank account number. The broker opens the trading account and the demat locker together, as one form. A day or two later he gets a 16-character demat number and a login.

He moves ₹1,600 from his bank to the trading account, buys 1 share, and checks the demat that evening. Empty. The share lands the next working day, and it shows up in the locker, not in the app's wallet.

cards.prompt: Meera has ₹2,000 in her bank and wants to buy her first share this week. Which order of steps is right?

options.text: Move money into the demat account, place the order, the share lands in the trading account.
Move money from the bank to the trading account, place the order, the share lands in the demat account.
Place the order straight from her bank app, the share lands in the trading account.

whyNot.a: That's the locker doing the purse's job: the demat account holds shares, never cash. Money goes to the trading account.
whyNot.c: That's skipping the counter: a bank app cannot place orders on the exchange. Only a broker's trading account can.

cards.reteach: Follow the rupee. It leaves the purse (bank), stops at the counter (trading account), and buys a share. The share then goes into the locker (demat). Cash never enters the demat, and shares never sit in the trading account.

cards.title: KYC, and what the counter costs
cards.body:
Before opening your accounts, a broker must run *KYC*, short for know your customer: SEBI's check that your PAN, the tax number, and your Aadhaar match a bank account in your name. So never hand your PAN and Aadhaar to a stranger who offers to 'set it up for you'.

Three charges to look for. An opening fee, often ₹0. A yearly demat maintenance charge for keeping the locker, usually a few hundred rupees. And *brokerage*, the fee per order: many brokers charge ₹0 when you buy shares to hold, and a flat fee of around ₹20 for same-day trades. **The locker fee is yearly; brokerage is per order.**

Sunil's college friend 'trades for a group'. Sunil sends him ₹25,000 on UPI, gets WhatsApp screenshots of profits, and never opens a demat account of his own. A year later the friend stops replying. There were no shares in Sunil's name, so there was nothing to claim. **The tell: if you cannot log in and see the share in a demat account with your name on it, you do not own it.**

cards.prompt: At a wedding, a cousin says: 'Your broker app keeps your shares. If the app goes bust, so do they.' Which reply is right?

options.text: True, which is why you should spread shares across three apps.
Not quite. Shares sit in a demat account at NSDL or CDSL, in my name. The app only places orders.
Not quite. Shares are backed up in my bank account.

whyNot.a: That's treating the runner as the locker: the app places orders, so more apps only means more counters. The share's home is the demat, not the app.
whyNot.c: That's the purse, not the locker: a bank account holds rupees. Shares are electronic entries at a depository, never at a bank.

cards.reteach: Picture the bazaar at closing time. The runner goes home, the stalls shut, and your locker is still there with your share inside. The locker belongs to NSDL or CDSL and carries your name. The broker only had a key to open it for you.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Your bank holds the cash, your trading account is the broker's counter where you place orders, and your demat account is the locker at NSDL or CDSL that holds your shares in your name. **The broker opens the locker; it never owns what's inside.**

Tomorrow: why a ₹3,000 share can cost you less than a ₹50 one.

Tonight, open the website of one SEBI-registered broker. Find two numbers: its SEBI registration number and its yearly demat maintenance charge. Write both down. Don't open an account yet; just see what the counter costs.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now open a demat and trading account and say which account holds your shares and which holds your cash.
